sourceEvidence.label: Zeus Phase H source and deployment security boundaries

assessment.summary: The current boundary is suitable for local and pre-production use; production should bind key delivery and outbound authority to the selected cloud environment.

nonNegotiables: No secret value may enter logs, events, traces, OpenAPI responses, or repository files.
Zeus remains cloud-only and provider-neutral until a production cloud is selected.
OIDC and model providers require controlled HTTPS egress.
assumptions: No cloud provider, KMS product, egress gateway, or workload identity implementation has been selected.
No production latency or KMS quota measurement is available.

opportunities.title: Bind secret delivery and outbound authority to the production environment
opportunities.summary: Keep the application boundary provider-neutral while making key delivery and HTTPS destinations explicit deployment controls.
opportunities.diagnosis: The process accepts a protected key file, but the baseline still relies on a Kubernetes Secret and permits TCP 443 to any destination because provider endpoints are unknown.

evidence.claim: The process accepts one regular envelope-key file, rejects symlinks, limits its size, and rejects group or other access bits on Unix.
Secret encryption is owned by an EnvelopeCipher trait; the current implementation keeps one AES-256-GCM master key in process memory.
A non-root init container stages the Secret source into a memory-backed regular 0400 file for the API, which has a read-only root filesystem; the HTTPS egress rule still has no destination selector.
A compromised API process would inherit both decrypted secret access and broad HTTPS reach, so those authorities should be narrowed by the production environment.

desiredInvariants: Every production envelope key originates from an approved KMS-backed delivery path and never appears in an environment variable.
Only the zeus-api Pod can read the mounted key, and a rollout can select a new key id without rewriting historical ciphertext in place.
Provider, OIDC, KMS, and telemetry traffic can reach only approved destinations through an observable egress control.
Loss of KMS or secret delivery fails readiness before Zeus accepts secret-dependent traffic.

options.title: KMS-backed mounted key with controlled egress
options.summary: Use workload identity and the cloud secret driver to mount a KMS-protected key, while an egress gateway owns destination allowlists.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The existing file seam is the application-side enforcement point.
Key delivery improves, while the master key still exists in process memory during the Pod lifetime.
A cloud overlay must replace broad HTTPS egress with gateway-routed allowlists.
A compromised API retains necessary model and secret authority, but the reachable destinations become bounded and observable.

tradeoffs.assessment: The key leaves environment variables and destination policy moves out of application convention; Pod memory remains a trusted boundary.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Verify workload identity, SecretProviderClass policy, file mode, Pod access denial, egress deny logs, and key rotation in the target cluster.

tradeoffs.assessment: Encryption remains local AES-GCM; egress gateway latency affects remote calls only.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare model, OIDC, and telemetry p95 latency with and without the gateway under the capacity workload.

tradeoffs.assessment: The process retains the same 32-byte master key and cipher state.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare API Pod RSS before and after enabling the secret driver and gateway sidecars, if any.

tradeoffs.assessment: A missing key fails startup, while secret-driver and gateway availability become deployment dependencies.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Restart Pods during KMS denial, secret rotation, gateway restart, and DNS failure; verify readiness and lease recovery.

tradeoffs.assessment: Platform owners must operate workload identity, the secret driver, allowlists, and rotation alerts.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run the key-rotation and provider-outage procedures with the on-call team.

tradeoffs.assessment: The application already reads a file, so the cloud overlay can change delivery without changing stored envelopes.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Deploy one canary Pod with the mounted key, read existing ciphertext, write a test secret, then roll back to the prior Secret source.

residualRisks: A compromised API process can read the active master key from memory.
A mistaken gateway allowlist can block OIDC or Provider access or permit an unintended host.
Kubernetes administrators with Secret or node access remain highly privileged.

workPackages: Keep the strict file-loading seam and remove inline production key configuration.
Add the selected cloud secret-driver and workload-identity overlay.
Route HTTPS through an approved egress gateway and install destination policies.
Exercise rotation, denial, restart, and rollback procedures.
acceptanceCriteria: No production Pod receives the envelope key through an environment variable.
An unlabelled Pod cannot read the key or reach Provider, OIDC, telemetry, or KMS endpoints.
Zeus reads existing envelopes before and after one key-delivery rotation.
The 200-Run capacity gate stays within its queue-wait target.
migrationNotes: Select a cloud and secret driver before writing environment-specific manifests.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Restore the prior Secret volume source and gateway policy while retaining the same key id and ciphertext.

options.title: Direct KMS envelope encryption
options.summary: Use workload identity to ask KMS to wrap per-secret data keys and persist the encrypted data key with each envelope.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The static key file disappears after every ciphertext has a KMS-wrapped data key.
A new asynchronous cipher boundary and envelope format are required.
KMS gets a narrow destination and workload identity, while Provider and OIDC egress still need allowlists.
No long-lived master key is mounted, but a compromised process can still request decrypt operations within its KMS policy.

tradeoffs.assessment: The Pod loses a static master key; KMS authorization, request context, quotas, and audit logs become the main control plane.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prove KMS policy separation, encryption-context binding, denied cross-tenant decrypt, rotation, and KMS audit coverage.

tradeoffs.assessment: Cold decrypt and key generation add a network call; caching data keys trades latency for a longer plaintext lifetime.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Benchmark secret write and cold/warm read p50, p95, p99 under 200 concurrent Runs and set a cache policy from measured results.

tradeoffs.assessment: Removing one master key is small; SDK pools and optional data-key caches may increase retained memory.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure Pod RSS with caching disabled and with the proposed bounded cache.

tradeoffs.assessment: Secret reads depend on KMS availability and quotas unless carefully bounded caches are accepted.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inject KMS timeout, throttling, permission denial, and regional outage; confirm fail-closed behavior and Run recovery.

tradeoffs.assessment: The team owns KMS policy, SDK telemetry, quota alarms, encrypted-data-key migrations, and emergency access procedures.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run a game day with platform, security, database, and Zeus on-call owners.

tradeoffs.assessment: The synchronous trait and stored envelope lack an encrypted data key, so code, schema, dual-read, and rewrap work are required.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Migrate a copied production-shaped dataset with dual-read, canary writes, restart, rollback, and checksum verification.

residualRisks: A compromised API can call KMS while its workload identity remains valid.
Incorrect encryption context or tenant policy can create cross-tenant decrypt risk.
KMS throttling can block login, Provider access, and Capability execution.

workPackages: Select one cloud KMS and define tenant-bound encryption context.
Make secret operations asynchronous and add a KMS-backed implementation.
Version the stored envelope and add encrypted data-key fields.
Ship dual-read and new-write migration before rewrapping historical rows.
acceptanceCriteria: No static envelope master key is mounted in the API Pod.
Cross-tenant decrypt is denied by both application context and KMS policy.
KMS outage and throttling produce stable errors without secret disclosure or duplicate side effects.
All historical envelopes survive dual-read migration and rollback.
migrationNotes: Do not start schema work before selecting the KMS provider and availability target.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Keep old envelopes and the mounted-key reader until new writes, reads, rewrap, and rollback have completed in a production-shaped environment.

opportunities.recommendation: Use the mounted-key design for 0.1.0 because it fits the existing seam and keeps the cloud choice outside application code. Revisit direct KMS when the cloud, KMS SLO, quota, and measured secret-read budget are known.

openQuestions: Which cloud, KMS, Secret CSI or external-secret controller, workload identity, and egress gateway will production use?
What KMS outage behavior and secret-read latency budget can the enterprise accept?
Will Organization isolation require separate KMS keys or encryption contexts?
